extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific_method, logic, and philosophy_of_science
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of criteria and principles for inductive reasoning and causal attribution in scientific inquiry, including distinctions between description and explanation, conditions for valid induction, and how causes compose or exclude one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of general propositions in scientific inference
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, the inference must necessarily pass through the intermediate stage of a general proposition, because Science wants its conclusions for record, and not for instantaneous use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical inferences used for immediate action may not be articulated as generalizations yet can be inductive; scientific conclusions, however, should be expressible as general propositions for reproducibility and record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Description and Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Description merely represents facts or the manner of occurrence; an Explanation ascribes a mechanism or physical agent responsible for the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions can be modes of representing facts without claiming a cause; explanations assert material facts or agents and may be subject to truth/falsity (e.g., a hypothesis framed merely as a representation would be reconcilable with another theory, whereas an explanation invoking a physical agent may contradict another explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual exclusivity of conflicting explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different explanations of the same fact which ascribe incompatible mechanisms cannot both be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vortices vs Newtonian gravitation vs an 'inherent virtue' — if one explanation attributes motion to a physical agent and another to a universal law incompatible in mechanism, they exclude one another. Similar contrasts: emission vs undulatory theories of light; single vs double electricities; rival accounts of volcanic action or origins of organic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting predictions cannot both be true
rubrics_metrics.description: If two theories produce incompatible predictions about the same phenomenon, both predictions cannot be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use predictions as a decisive test: e.g., different periodicities predicted for a comet, or historical predictions about navigation and steam power — incompatible forecasts indicate mutually exclusive theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of nature as a condition for valid induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition of the validity of every induction is that there be uniformity in the course of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uniformity underlies the expectation that past observed regularities will continue; it is a foundational presumption for making inductive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-limited uniformity suffices for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that uniformity should pervade all nature; it is enough that it pervades the particular class of phenomena to which the induction relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An induction concerning planetary motion or magnetism can be valid even if other domains (e.g., weather) are irregular; early science relied on class-specific regularities rather than a presumption of universal order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction implies either prior or newly established general fact
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction implies either that the general fact (uniformity) is already known, or that we are now entitled to conclude it from the same evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing a general conclusion from instances, either we rely on previously established generality, or we establish it now from accumulated instances (example: concluding 'the Duke of Wellington is mortal' presumes either a prior universal or establishes it from observed cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad induction arises from spurious correlations and prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs like superstitions are often regarded as conclusions from experience, but rest on improper interpretation of coincidences or antecedent prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: belief that crops require sowing in a certain lunar phase; such conclusions are inductive in form but are 'bad induction' due to causal misattribution or insufficient evidence. Preconceptions can predispose interpretation of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting what to call 'the cause' depends on informativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary discourse the condition called the cause is typically that element of the antecedents which the hearer may reasonably need to be informed of — i.e., the informative or relevant antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of bodily organs is a necessary condition for death by poison but not given as the cause because it supplies no useful information; conversely, citing a sentinel's absence vs the bribe that caused it may both be called causes depending on which condition explains what is informative or in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate events vs antecedent states in causal language
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions which are antecedent states (long-standing conditions) are rarely spoken of as causes unless they are the unknown or explanatory factor; proximate antecedent events are more often cited as causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: muscles are not usually called the cause of a leap (they are necessary states), whereas the immediate event enabling the leap is cited; when the unknown condition is negative or contrastive, it may be singled out as cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative conditions and absence of counteracting causes counted as causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative conditions (the absence of some counteracting cause) may be properly called the cause when they are the explanatory circumstance that makes the effect occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'died for want of medical advice' or 'drowned because he could not swim' — the negative condition is explanatory because it distinguishes the case; Mill also formulates a formula including negative conditions as absence of counteracting causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active force is not a necessary criterion for calling something a cause
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not required that the element named as cause be the one exerting 'active force' in a popular sense; conditions that supply the necessary context are often called causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: saying a man fell because his foot slipped vs because of his weight — the popular attribution may focus on the informative condition rather than the element exerting force. Opening flood-gates is called the cause of a flow though the active force is the water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes and apparent exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes combine (compose) to produce effects; apparent counterexamples (e.g., two sparks vs one, a double dose of medicine) often reflect attention to remote versus immediate effects or to collocation thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doubling a cause may not double the immediately observed effect when a certain collocation once obtained suffices for the full effect; distinguishing immediate vs remote effects (and heteropathic laws) resolves many alleged exceptions. Examples discussed include gunpowder sparks, doses of medicine, and collocations that enable a prime mover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive properties as special cases of causal accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Some properties (e.g., opacity) appear purely preventive and seem exceptions to composition of causes, but they need not invalidate causal formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opacity defeats the passage of light and thus acts by preventing another agency's effect; such cases may be practically accommodated by regarding them as absence or counteraction rather than genuine exceptions to causal composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of causal principles to human will and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Human actions and volitions are accounted for by motives and character; saying actions 'necessarily' follow from character means they invariably do so and would be predictable by someone who knew the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that applying causation to human behavior is not incompatible with consciousness; it does not imply Asiatic fatalism but rather predictability given sufficient knowledge of character and motives.
